lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved dispute-form completion by 40% by splitting the form into three short steps with saved progress.
- Brought the design system to WCAG 2.1 AA by setting body-text contrast to at least 3:1 against every background.
- Built a research repository of 250 tagged session clips that product managers searched before writing new requirements.
- Presented quarterly findings to the head of product and two design teams; three of the top five recommended fixes shipped in the next release cycle.
- Validated the redesigned app navigation's findability with an open card sort of 30 customers before it shipped.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Apr 2020 - Feb 2022
- Owned the monthly patient survey and the reporting dashboard the care teams used.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Wrote the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.

- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients while also running the team's recruiting calendar, updating the style guide, onboarding two interns and taking notes for the accessibility working group, which cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Championed an inclusive, human-centered design approach to transit wayfinding that delivered meaningful, user-first outcomes.
- Measured the redesign with timed tasks: median route-finding time fell from 95 to 62 seconds and errors from 11 to 3 across the 12 sessions.
- Published the design files and test protocol openly, and the city's transit agency invited the project to its spring accessibility review.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Tested three onboarding prototypes with 24 new customers and shipped the design that lifted completed sign-ups by 41% in its first quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA), Tableau
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interviews, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: Education appears before experience despite several years of relevant work.
items.because: The degree leads before the roles that establish the candidate’s career direction.

items.says: The 10-month gap between the degree and the first listed role is unexplained.
The 40% increase has no starting rate or stated calculation basis.
A 3:1 contrast ratio does not meet WCAG 2.1 AA for normal body text.
items.because: Normal text requires at least 4.5:1; 3:1 applies to large text.

items.says: The repository’s use is described, but not what that use changed.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether it informed a decision or improved requirements.

items.says: The long relative clause delays the repository’s practical value.
The shipped fixes appear after the presentation details.
items.because: The result is easy to miss.

items.says: An open card sort does not validate findability in a proposed navigation.
items.because: It shows how participants group and label content, not whether they can find items.

items.says: The claimed findability validation gives no finding or resulting decision.
items.because: Readers cannot tell what customers found or how the research informed the navigation.

items.says: “Findability” is jargon.
items.because: It may slow readers outside UX research.

items.says: “Before it shipped” adds an unnecessary ending.
The sign-up result is buried after the research details, and “The shipped design” makes it less direct.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the measurable change at the end.

items.says: The survey and dashboard are presented as responsibilities without a concrete action or approach.
items.because: “Owned” does not show what the candidate did or how they did it.

items.says: The line does not say what the survey or dashboard helped care teams do.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether the work informed a decision or action.

items.says: The appointment-reminder outcome appears after the interview detail.
items.because: The missed-appointment reduction is the clearest impact but comes after the setup.

items.says: The duty list interrupts the testing-and-result story, burying the 30% outcome.
items.because: The unrelated duties break the link between testing and the support-call result.

items.says: The testing detail does not say what patients were asked to do or what the test revealed.
The 30% support-call reduction has no comparison period or baseline.
The opening uses broad claims instead of a design practice or concrete outcome.
items.because: The labels do not show what was done or what changed for riders.

items.says: The strongest result is not at the start of the bullet.
items.because: Starting with the measurement setup makes readers wait for the evidence of impact.

items.says: “Openly” repeats what publishing the files and protocol already conveys.
The booking-flow result lacks a specific design change.
The phone-booking drop lacks a comparison basis.
The six fixes are described without saying whether booking completion improved afterward.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether the fixes changed the user outcome.

items.says: The 41% sign-up increase lacks a baseline or comparison.
items.because: Readers cannot tell how the lift was calculated.

items.says: “New customers” conflicts with the clinic-patient group named above.
items.because: The change makes the project’s participant group sound inconsistent.
